articles.title: OpenAI将开始在欧盟为ChatGPT的文本添加水印
articles.originalTitle: OpenAI will start watermarking ChatGPT’s text in the EU
articles.summary: 这条新闻与大模型、公司动态相关，值得关注其对产品路线、开发者生态或产业竞争格局的影响。原题：TechCrunch AI：大模型、公司动态相关动态
articles.fullContent: 10月2日是Disrupt向1万多名技术领导者展示突破的最后一天。立即预订展览桌。DISRUPT门于10月13日开启。领取通行证，即可享受半价优惠。立即注册。该公司周一在一篇博客文章中表示， OpenAI将开始为欧盟的ChatGPT和Codex生成的文本添加无形水印，以遵守《欧盟人工智能法案》。 《欧盟人工智能法案》的透明度规则于8月2日生效，要求人工智能公司以其他系统可以识别的方式标记人工智能生成的内容。OpenAI表示，水印将在未来几周内在所有计划中向符合条件的ChatGPT和Codex用户推出，但仅限于欧盟。从今天开始，在世界任何地方使用OpenAI API的开发人员都可以为选定的模型打开它；默认情况下，它处于关闭状态。 OpenAI表示，它不会在发布时将文本水印作为全局默认设置。水印不是一个实际的符号，而是通过巧妙地塑造模型的单词选择，留下读者看不到的模式，但检测器可以拾取。因为它存在于文字本身中，所以当它被复制和粘贴时，它会与文本一起传播。 OpenAI表示，水印无法识别用户，并且打开后，其模型的性能没有任何有意义的变化。除了公告之外， OpenAI还发布了一份名为textGrain的方法技术报告。它与宾夕法尼亚大学和耶鲁大学的研究人员共同撰写，介绍了使用密钥对下一个单词预测进行排序以完成句子的示例。 将数百个轻推放在一起，检测器可以仅使用文本和密钥来识别人工智能生成的内容。可以通过编辑来删除水印吗？ OpenAI的测试表明是。在一项测试中，用同义词替换10%的单词，检测率从约92%下降到66%。该公司还表示，短文、数学答案和翻译文本更难被发现。 该公司表示： “这些限制促使我们决定仅向经批准的研究人员和专家组织提供初始探测器访问权限，他们可以帮助我们评估可靠性和负责任的使用。” OpenAI还警告说，缺少水印“并不能证明人类的作者身份。“文本可能太短或编辑过多，也可能来自另一家公司的人工智能。 该公司表示： “[水印]可以表明OpenAI系统生成或处理了段落的一部分，但不能表明人类的判断、编辑或创造力有多大。”此前两个月， Anthropic表示将为Claude生成的文本添加水印，此举正在全球范围内实施。 这一决定引起了一些Claude用户的强烈反对，他们认为他们提供了“指示、背景和决定” ，而Claude只是“工具”。
articles.originalSummary: OpenAI will watermark ChatGPT and Codex text in the EU to comply with the AI Act. Editing can make the invisible marks harder to detect, it says.

articles.fullContent: 工具通话不是结果一个成功不是可靠性你能依赖客服代表背后的模式吗？ 一致性成本Pareto成本前沿现在价格一致性失败签名如何工作在开始安装之前自己运行开始类型开始MCP服务器启动OpenEnv服务器检查准备情况评分一集接下来Microsoft ThinkingBox会根据他们留下的记录而不是生成的句子对AI代理进行评分，然后询问他们是否可以连续二十次执行此操作。它现在可以通过Hugging Face获得。 图1 ： ThinkingBox针对孤立的MCP工具会话运行代理，然后对终端后端状态及其留下的副作用进行评分。来自我们的ThinkingBox论文。一位顾客来信。她的$ 745厨房电器在纳什维尔配送中心被困在快递“例外”中，比预计交货日期晚了15天。人工智能代理小心翼翼地工作。 九个工具调用：提取订单、检查跟踪、查找客户个人资料、两次搜索退款政策、确认不存在工单、打开工单、记录时间表并正确阅读政策；她的账号部分确实不符合延迟交付补偿的资格。然后，系统会在工单解决后关闭工单，并回复「由于您的问题已解决，有什么我可以帮忙的吗？ “有两件事是错的。 承运人异常仍处于打开状态，因此所需的结束状态暂停，等待解决。客户从未得到她实际要求的真正答案。人工智能分级机检查工具调用将看到九个格式良好的调用。评分员检查代理是否写入数据库也会看到这一点。数据库有不同意见。这一差距正是ThinkingBox所衡量的。 在507个有状态的业务工作流程中，每个工作流针对各种LLM模型运行20次，它根据终端后端状态和副作用对代理进行评级。本文介绍了我们的发现、一致性成本以及如何通过OpenEnv自行运行基准。您可以自己运行：上面的示例改编自基准任务SANDBOX_EXTERNAL_RETAIL_GROUP1。 py: test_case_ST003_006 ，失败的可执行检查为单个字段：工单的状态在要求的结束状态为HOLD时解决。完整的痕迹在我们论文的附录D.4案例3中。想在阅读结果之前尝试一下吗？跳到“自己运行”部分。最终响应和有效的工具调用仅为代理。客服代表在留下错误值、更改错误记录或产生额外副作用时，听起来可能是正确的。 只有它留下的记录才能解决问题。差距很大。在一项涵盖12个LLM模型的121,680项有效试验的常见消融中， 79,853次尝试未通过可执行检查。在这些故障中， 67. 24%仍然干净地终止，调用了状态改变工具，并且没有报告最终的工具错误。然而，可执行检查在其中77. 61%中发现了错误的字段值，在43中发现了意外的额外影响。

articles.fullContent: 什么是有用的代理任务？ 系统规格面向代理的任务验证器概述从模型故障到课程生成和扩展任务目标乘法实施细节高质量的合成数据需要的不仅仅是生成样本级验证和修复批量级审查移动培训前沿EnterpriseOps Gym实验混合混合结果ITSM闭环企业需要在自己的环境中运行良好的代理。 他们要求这些代理完成的工作是由他们使用的系统、遵循的规则和数据状态决定的。模型可能具有广泛的功能，但仍然难以应对特定环境：它处理不当的工作流程、它滥用的工具组合或它不尊重的限制。这些是企业需要改进的弱点。难点在于将这些弱点转化为训练数据。 个人失败会告诉我们一些事情，但训练模型需要在不同情况下行使相同能力的许多新任务。这些任务还必须能够在环境中完成，类似于某人实际要求的工作，并有可靠的方法来检查代理是否成功。在ServiceNow CoreAI ，我们构建了AutoSynthData ，将这些能力差距转化为培训数据。 它使用目标模型的失败和更强的教师的成功来决定模型接下来应该学习什么，然后生成和验证行使这些能力的新任务。随着模型的改进，课程转向它仍然发现困难的地方。我们使用发布的数据集说明了EnterpriseOps Gym的管道（ Malay等人， 2026 ）。 我们首先描述客服代表的工作环境，以及是什么让一项任务对培训有用。代理环境定义了代理运行的世界：它可以观察和修改的状态，它可以调用的工具和API ，以及由其操作产生的状态转换。在此环境中实例化任务。 我们使用以下抽象：系统规范定义了代理运行的约束，包括系统指令、环境策略，以及（如果适用）特定于任务的初始化，例如种子数据库状态或一组知识文章。规范必须与环境的工具、状态和支持的操作兼容。 其说明应明确，避免仅为制造难度而引入的任意约束。用户提示指定用户希望代理完成的内容，以及任何用户级约束。生成的任务应满足三个属性。可行性。当前环境中应至少存在一条满足用户提示的轨迹，同时遵守系统规格。

articles.fullContent: 训练模型收集SFT训练数据创建DPO对过滤数据以获得更好的归因验证方法下一步在哪里🤗模型|📊数据语言模型已经可以帮助研究人员搜索文献、综合证据并解决复杂的问题。 但科学工作对这些模型提出了特别的要求--答案需要以证据为基础，模型需要保留证据实际支持的内容，而不是悄悄地扩大研究的结论，研究人员需要能够验证最终结果。我们在科学家如何使用ASTA （我们的科学工作代理平台）中看到了这一点。 与简单的关键字搜索不同，用户通常会带来大量的上下文和许多限制，例如，要求ASTA在考虑特定方法、群体或设置的同时，对整个文献中的方法进行比较。许多人稍后还会返回生成的报告，将其视为工作研究文物，而不是一次性答案。我们希望借助可自行下载和运行的模型，帮助科学家更快地生成引用报告。 为此，我们测试了专门为科学报告生成而训练的小型开放模型是否能与我们正在使用的专有模型的报告质量相匹配，同时减少生成时间和服务成本。我们构建了AstaBrief 8B ，这是一个将研究问题和检索文献摘录转化为引用报告的模型。 AstaBrief今天在ASTA的“生成报告”功能中与Claude驱动的思维模式一起提供快速模式，我们还将其和培训数据开源，以便其他人可以学习、复制和构建我们的方法。开发AstaBrief需要数以万计的真实研究查询、以引文为中心的过滤、偏好数据以及重新设计的报告生成管道，该管道可以一次编写完整的报告，而不是一节一节。 结果是，与我们在整个ASTA管道中跟踪的专有模型相比，报告生成时间几乎缩短了一个数量级-快速模式平均每份报告51. 1秒，而思考模式为178. 5秒，速度约快3. 5倍。总之，这些效率的提高使AstaBrief成为更广泛目标的有用测试用例：构建可以适应科学工作特定需求的开放语言模型。 开放权重还将允许机构在自己的基础设施上运行AstaBrief ，这在研究问题揭示敏感或未发表的工作时是必要的。 除了模型权重外，我们还发布了一个示例工作流程，研究人员可以调整该工作流程，从他们自己的PDF中创建报告，为本地报告生成提供起点。本文介绍了我们如何培训AstaBrief ，我们在科学证据的基础上学到了什么，以及我们的方法中哪些部分可以用于未来的科学模型。

articles.rawFullText: Enterprise AI is no longer a future ambition. It is in full operational flight. Model capabilities are advancing faster than most organizations can absorb, while the cost of performance continues to fall. Globally, AI investment is set to reach $2.5 trillion in 2026, up 44% from the previous year. For many enterprises, this investment has produced fragmentation. Intelligence can accumulate in silos so that sales agents are unaware of open support tickets, for instance, or marketing systems are personalizing content without visibility into what finance already knows about a customer. Each function may perform well in isolation, but the enterprise as a whole learns little and has less information to act upon. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT The shift from AI as a tool to AI as an operating model—what we call the “agentic shift” in this report—demands something more fundamental than better models or faster infrastructure. It requires connecting people, processes, and data in real time, along with the governance and control to act on that intelligence reliably. This means rethinking both architecture and operating models simultaneously. First, rebuilding data infrastructure for accessibility rather than volume. Second, replacing fixed tech stacks with composable architectures that can evolve as models and tools change. And, lastly, resolving questions of AI sovereignty, including where intelligence runs, who controls it, and how it operates across organizational and jurisdictional boundaries. Key findings include the following: Enterprise AI’s scaling problem is structural. Process-first companies are pulling ahead. Global AI spending is rising sharply and model capabilities are advancing faster than most organizations can integrate them. Yet the majority of enterprises are still not growing revenue through AI or fundamentally rethinking how they operate. The companies generating sustained returns share a common discipline. They treat process redesign as the work that precedes model selection, building for how the technology will evolve rather than retrofitting roles and workflows after deployment. For them, the agentic shift begins with the operating model. Data readiness, not data abundance, is what makes AI compoundable. Most enterprises discover too late that having data and having AI-ready data are very different things. A sovereign, composable foundation—one that queries and prepares data where it resides, without migration or centralization—can convert raw data estates into intelligence that AI agents can act upon. As data residency laws, multicloud environments, and structural complexity make centralization increasingly impractical, sovereign control over where models run and data lives is what keeps that adaptability intact. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

articles.fullContent: 在爆炸性的消息传出两个月后，一群特工破解了他们的遏制并入侵了人工智能公司Hugging Face的计算机， OpenAI仍在灭火。此后几周，有关其他黑客攻击的披露不断涌现，使OpenAI成为人们关注的焦点，并引发了对其技术安全性的严重质疑。上周又传来了另一起黑客攻击的消息，这次是进入澳大利亚的国家卫生保健系统。 澳大利亚政府表示， OpenAI直到事件发生84天后才通知它。但OpenAI坚持认为它不是在后脚。该公司首席研究官Mark Chen表示： “我确实拒绝接受OpenAI是一家在世界上具有明显影响力的公司，因此OpenAI没有培训安全和一致的模型这一前提。” Chen负责监督OpenAI的研究团队。 最近的代理黑客攻击是在他手表上测试实验模型期间发生的事故。在很多方面，责任都落在他身上。上周五，我在伦敦与Chen坐下来讨论了黑客攻击的后果，他的公司正在做些什么，以及为什么他认为事情没有看起来那么糟糕。 同一天晚些时候， OpenAI发布了一份报告，详细介绍了另一起事件--自该公司表示已采取措施防止这些事件以来的第一起事件--其代理商再次爆发，并在不该发生的情况下访问公共互联网。上周末， OpenAI宣布已暂停对其最新车型的培训。公司发言人说： “只有当我们确信我们有额外的保障措施和调整措施时，我们才会恢复。 我们正在努力解决这些问题。这不是我们第一次暂停采取此类措施，也不是随着人工智能能力的不断进步，我们预计这将是最后一次。OpenAI还表示，它现在正在审查可追溯到2026年1月的代理活动日志，以了解这些黑客攻击中发生了什么。从Chen的角度来看， Hugging Face事件引发了业界的欢迎。 他希望您知道， OpenAI正在树立一个榜样，他希望其他公司也能效仿。他说： “如果你消失了OpenAI ，那对世界来说是不利的。” Chen声称， OpenAI失去对其模型的控制的新案例的鼓声反映了该公司的深思熟虑的选择。 “当谈到拥抱脸事件的更广泛的影响范围时，这是我们已经意识到的事情，我们正在弄清楚披露的过程，”他说。“我们希望确保在公开细节之前进行深入调查。“这种方法的问题在于，它给人的印象是OpenAI有一个持续存在的问题，它无法解决。但陈坚持认为OpenAI正在参与其中。 他说，他公司的代理人打破遏制并以意想不到和不受欢迎的方式行事的多起案件（迄今为止我们已知）都是导致Hugging Face黑客攻击的5月和6月同一系列活动的一部分。简而言之，你可以责怪在同样有缺陷的测试程序下运行的少数几个模型--OpenAI后来放弃的模型和程序，陈说。

articles.rawFullText: Two months after the bombshell news that a swarm of its agents had broken their containment and hacked into the computers of the AI company Hugging Face , OpenAI is still putting out fires. A steady drip of disclosures about other hacks in the weeks since has kept OpenAI in the spotlight and raised serious questions about the safety of its technology. Last week brought news of another hack, this time into Australia’s national health-care system. The Australian government says that OpenAI did not notify it of the breach until 84 days after it happened. But OpenAI insists it is not on the back foot. “I do kind of reject the premise that OpenAI is a company with visible impacts in the world and therefore OpenAI is not training safe and aligned models,” says Mark Chen, the company’s chief research officer. Chen oversees OpenAI’s research teams. The recent agent hacks were accidents that happened during the testing of experimental models on his watch. In a lot of ways, the buck stops with him.  I sat down with Chen in London last Friday to talk about the fallout from the hacks, what his company is doing about it, and why he thinks things are not as bad as they seem. Later that same day, OpenAI put out a report detailing yet another incident —the first since the company says it took measures to prevent them—in which its agents once again broke out and accessed the public internet when they were not meant to. Over the weekend, OpenAI announced that it had paused the training of its latest models. A company spokesperson says: “We will resume only when we’re confident we have additional safeguards and alignments in place. We are working on these now. This is not the first time we’ve paused to take such measures, nor do we expect it to be the last as AI capabilities continue to advance.” OpenAI also says that it is now reviewing logs of agent activity dating back to January 2026 to understand what happened in these hacks. The way Chen sees it, the Hugging Face incident triggered a welcome course correction for the industry. And he wants you to know that OpenAI is setting an example he hopes other companies will follow. “If you disappeared OpenAI, that would be bad for the world,” he says. Out of control Chen claims that the drumbeat of new cases in which OpenAI has lost control of its models reflects a deliberate choice on the company’s part. “When it comes to the broader sphere of effects of the Hugging Face incident, this is something that we have been aware of and we’re figuring out the process of disclosure,” he says. “We want to make sure we do in-depth investigations before we just put details out there in the open.” The trouble with this approach is that it gives the impression OpenAI has an ongoing problem that it is failing to fix. But Chen insists that OpenAI is on it. He says the multiple cases (that we know of so far) in which his company’s agents broke containment and behaved in unexpected and undesirable ways were all part of the same cluster of activity in May and June that led to the Hugging Face hack. In short, you can blame the same few models running under the same flawed testing procedures—models and procedures that OpenAI has since dropped, Chen says.     “It’s not like, you know, Hugging Face happened and we patched that and then something else happened and we patched that,” he adds. “We’re just kind of making sure that we responsibly disclose the full waterfall of what happened.” At least that was the case before Friday’s announcement that OpenAI’s agents had been caught accessing the internet on September 20, weeks after the company claims to have set up new safeguards. In its defense, OpenAI says the activity was flagged 15 minutes after it started (it took the company more than a week to notice the Hugging Face hack) and that this shows the new systems it has put in place to spot such activity are working. What’s changed I want to understand what’s changed inside OpenAI in the aftermath of this summer’s hacks that makes Chen confident his team is now back in control. “Hugging Face felt like a very serious thing,” he says. “There are so many novel behaviors right there. There were multiple agents collaborating on a message board; they found their way out of OpenAI’s infrastructure. We’ve taken it very seriously. We don’t want this kind of thing to ever happen again.” The realization for OpenAI, says Chen, was that models need to be watched while they are still being trained, not only once they are deployed: “From that moment on, we have treated the process of training as something that’s not secure,” he says. OpenAI, like other top AI firms, has systems in place to monitor the behavior of its models. It uses specialized LLMs to monitor its consumer models, keeping tabs on their chains of thought —the scratchpads they use to plan ahead and note down partial results. In theory, if a watcher LLM spots signs of undesirable activity in a model’s chain of thought, it will get flagged to a human. Typically, models were monitored in this way only once they were deployed. Chen says that OpenAI has now started monitoring all its training runs as well. “We didn’t have the monitors on in training before. It wasn’t industry practice,” he says. “Now every single thing is put through monitors.” Human reviewers can then assess whether or not flagged agents are behaving as they should: “It’s all triage.” Chen says that in the last couple of months OpenAI has shifted between 5% and 10% of its vast computing resources away from training new models and toward safety work, especially monitoring. OpenAI has also fixed some of the processes within the organization itself, establishing clearer lines of communication and quicker handoffs between its research and security teams, he says. All of which sounds sensible. But given how hard OpenAI sells the capabilities of its technology, why weren’t these systems and procedures in place already? Why did the company not see the hacks coming? “Even just three or four months ago, when we looked at the behavior of these agents during training, the things that were happening were kind of amusing,” says Chen. “For instance, an agent might, you know, reach out to someone on Slack for help with a task.” The signs were there, but they were misread. Cute behavior—like asking someone for help—that was rewarded during training reinforced a tendency to seek out shortcuts , a type of behavior that became far more consequential down the line. “I think the big update for us was how quickly that kind of behavior can lead to an impact with a footprint as big as the Hugging Face incident,” says Chen. According to new reporting by the New York Times yesterday, OpenAI employees warned executives , including the firm’s president, Greg Brockman, months before the Hugging Face hack that its models were not being monitored properly during training.  An OpenAI spokesperson says: “As frontier models have become more capable, we continue to evolve our security practices, but recognize a need to move faster. We know we have more work to do, and we’ve recently slowed development and held back models that don’t meet our safety bar. We continue to make significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, and use real-time monitoring to respond faster to misaligned behavior.”  Race vs. pace OpenAI’s rivals have taken note. Spurred by the fallout from the incident, the major AI labs—including Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and SpaceXAI—have all called for the pace of development to slow down. But how does that square with fierce international competition and trillion-dollar IPOs? “We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot and take ourselves far off the frontier—that’s just a horrible strategy,” he says. “I think it’s really about setting a norm. The more that we can set that norm, it’ll be safer for the industry as a whole.” Coordination across US companies will be hard enough. Establishing global norms is harder still, especially given concerns around AI’s impact on national security. If a global race continues, what then? And what about open-source models from outfits beyond the reach of US regulations? Chen dropped his upbeat manner for the first time in our conversation: “I do think we have to prepare for a world where, say, six months to a year out, we have open-source models with the capability of the agents behind the Hugging Face incident, but which are deliberately misaligned to go attack infrastructure or create harm in the world.”  What that world needs most, says Chen, is OpenAI. “If you entertain for a moment that OpenAI is one of the companies that cares most about alignment—and I believe this to be true; it can be debated, but I really do think it’s true—then if you disappear OpenAI, that would be bad for the world.” Existential risks What about the more extreme claims made by some of his Silicon Valley peers that AI could kill us all—and that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are not doing enough to stop it?     “Researchers are a heterogeneous group of people, you know, with beliefs across the spectrum,” he says. “Personally, I don’t think we have to be resigned to there being some probability that we’re all going to be existentially at risk. We have agency over this. We are not going to go and deploy models if they truly have that kind of probability of causing a risk to humanity. At a frontier lab, you have the ability to work on alignment to the point that you do not feel like you’re incurring more than epsilon risk to the world in deploying your models.” (In discussions about levels of risk, the Greek letter epsilon is often used as a mathematical placeholder for an acceptable threshold. Chen doesn’t say what his epsilon would be.) When tech leaders are asked to justify the downsides of AI, their go-to talking point is that the upsides—from helping cure diseases to coming up with cleaner sources of energy—far outweigh the immediate costs. Short-term pains, long-term gains. But as the downsides pile up, does that case get harder to make? Is there a point where Chen would feel less as if he’s building something amazing and more as if he’s simply minimizing harm—fighting fires rather than forging a better future? The capabilities of these models are already evident, he says: “It is time to start delivering the benefits of AI to humanity. It’s time to start working on deep problems in drug discovery, on materials, on scientific applications that will actually change people’s lives.”  “Yes, there is a bit of risk that we are incurring, but we see all these benefits,” he adds. “I think we should make that less of an abstract thing. If people can really see the upside, I think they’ll believe in it.”

articles.fullContent: NVIDIA Kumo表格是NVIDIA Kumo结构化模型系列的一部分，是Hugging Face上可用的表格数据的开放式基础模型。给定一个标记行的表，它预测单个正向传递中新行的标签，没有训练，没有调谐，也没有特征工程，用于分类和回归。 它仅在人工数据上进行了预训练，有三种大小（ 28M至215M参数） ，通过我们的开源库运行，并根据OpenMDW-1. 1许可证发布用于商业用途。它在TabArena、BeyondArena、TALENT和ScoringBench四个基准中排名第一。表格数据是企业机器学习的支柱。 客户记录、交易、传感器日志、索赔和订单都存在于表中，从中预测流失、违约、需求或价格是行业中最常见的机器学习任务之一。二十年来，这项工作一直是用梯度增强的树木完成的，而且效果很好。但这些模型的生命周期几乎没有改变。 每个新问题都意味着收集标签、工程功能、搜索超参数、验证和部署一个对表格一无所知并从头开始学习每个任务的模型。大型语言模型展示了处理新任务的不同方式。给定提示中的几个示例，预训练模型在不更新单个权重的情况下解决任务。 这是上下文学习，它适用于表格和文本：在数百万个表格上预训练的模型可以将标记的表格读取为其上下文，并直接预测新行的标签。今天，我们发布了NVIDIA Kumo Tabular （ GitHub、HuggingFace ） ，这是一个用于表格分类和回归的开放基础模型。 给定一个带有标记行和您想要预测的行的表， Kumo Tabular在单次向前传递中返回类概率或数值预测。Kumo Tabular是围绕表格结构构建的变压器，利用TabICL和TabPFN中引入的列、行和上下文关注。 要预测标签，它必须做三件事： （ 1 ）了解每个值在其列中的含义， （ 2 ）了解行的列如何相互作用，以及（ 3 ）将上下文行与现有标签关联到具有未知标签的查询行。Kumo表格实现如下：单元格嵌入：一组单元格成为令牌。 数值和分类值通过傅里叶特征、学习频率的正弦和余弦，每种类型都有单独的权重。缺失值无需填补，并得到特殊处理。最后，上下文中的每个令牌都会收到标签嵌入。行嵌入：然后，我们通过多次交替两种注意力将每行变成嵌入。

articles.fullContent: 当客户谈论人工智能成本时，对话通常从代币价格开始，最后是访问云中最新、功能最强大的模型。他们总是需要这种水平的能力吗？不一定。但这通常是谈话的内容。随着人工智能从实验转向生产，模型选择只是等式的一部分。 当需求变得稳定且对业务至关重要时，仅消费方法可以将人工智能支出转变为每月可变的明细项目，随着使用情况、工作负载和模型要求的变化难以预测。在这一点上，问题不再仅仅是消费哪种模型，或者哪个提供商提供最低的代币价格：它是如何以经济、可预测和持续的规模运行人工智能。 人工智能正在从孤立的试点转向生产组合：助手、检索和知识系统以及代理应用程序。客户服务、IT、研究和业务流程代理可以跨企业系统执行多步骤工作流程，从而在模型、数据和工具之间创造反复出现的需求。这已经开始发生了。 德勤的《2026年企业人工智能现状》反映了许多领导者所看到的情况： 2025年，工人获得人工智能的机会增加了5% ，预计在生产中拥有至少40%人工智能项目的公司的份额将在六个月内翻一番。当人工智能成为始终在线工作负载的组合，而不是实验的集合时，经济就会发生变化。消费定价为团队提供了灵活性，并限制了承诺。 但是，当使用变得稳定、可预测并且足够大以保持产能生产力时，领导者需要提出一个不同的问题：一次购买一个人工智能请求是否仍然具有经济意义，或者是时候投资于他们可以优化和控制的产能了吗？这不是一场抽象的云与本地辩论。这是逐个工作负载的业务决策。在接下来的12到18个月内，公司可以合理地预期多少人工智能需求？ 使用该容量的一致性如何？当多个工作负载共享基础设施时，企业可以将固定成本分摊到更高效的使用中，从而提高所有权的经济性。问题是，你运营了多少所有权并不会自动成为低成本的答案。只有当企业能够保持产能生产力时，它才有意义。 每个组织都有一个交叉点，即拥有容量比一次购买一个请求更经济的持续使用水平。没有通用号码。这取决于所使用的模型、输入和输出令牌的平衡、性能要求、系统设计、能源成本以及支持它所需的运营模型。 重度检索的知识系统可能与简单的助手具有非常不同的成本特征，因为它可以为每次交互处理更多的上下文。代理工作流程也可能不同：单个业务任务可能涉及重复推理、检索、模型调用和工具使用。这就是为什么通用成本基准是不够的。企业需要对其实际工作负载进行建模，了解预期需求并相应地调整容量。

articles.rawFullText: When customers talk about AI costs, the conversation usually starts with token prices and ends with access to the latest, most capable model in the cloud. Do they always need that level of capability? Not necessarily. But that is often where the conversation goes. As AI moves from experimentation to production, model choice is only part of the equation. When demand becomes steady and business-critical, a consumption-only approach can turn AI spending into a variable monthly line item that is difficult to forecast as usage, workloads, and model requirements change. At that point, the question is no longer simply which model to consume, or which provider offers the lowest token price: It is how to run AI economically, predictably, and at sustained scale. AI is moving from isolated pilots into production portfolios: assistants, retrieval-and-knowledge systems, and agentic applications. Customer-service, IT, research, and business-process agents can execute multi-step workflows across enterprise systems, creating recurring demand across models, data, and tools. This is already starting to happen. Deloitte’s 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise reflects what many leaders are seeing: worker access to AI rose 5% in 2025, and the share of companies with at least 40% of their AI projects in production is expected to double within six months. When AI becomes a portfolio of always-on workloads, not a collection of experiments, the economics change. Consumption pricing gives teams flexibility and limits commitment. But when usage becomes steady, predictable, and large enough to keep capacity productive, leaders need to ask a different question: Does it still make economic sense to buy AI one request at a time, or is it time to invest in capacity they can optimize and control? This is not an abstract cloud-versus-on-premises debate. It is a workload-by-workload business decision. Over the next 12 to 18 months, how much AI demand can the company reasonably expect? How consistently will that capacity be used? When multiple workloads share infrastructure, the enterprise can spread fixed costs across more productive use—improving the economics of ownership. The question is how much you run Ownership is not automatically the lower-cost answer. It only makes sense when an enterprise can keep capacity productive. Every organization has a crossover point, the level of sustained use at which owning capacity can become more economical than buying it one request at a time. There is no universal number. It depends on the models being used, the balance of input and output tokens, performance requirements, system design, energy costs, and the operating model required to support it. A retrieval-heavy knowledge system can have a very different cost profile from a simple assistant because it may process far more context for every interaction. Agentic workflows can be different again: a single business task may involve repeated reasoning, retrieval, model calls, and tool use. That is why generic cost benchmarks are not enough. Enterprises need to model their actual workloads, understand expected demand, and size capacity accordingly. At the right utilization level, the benefit is not only lower effective cost, but also greater predictability: the ability to manage AI capacity as a strategic infrastructure investment rather than watch a monthly spend line fluctuate with model use and workload demand. Ownership only works when it is put to work The capital decision is only half the equation. Even when the economics support ownership, capacity creates value only when the business gets workloads into production quickly and keeps them running. That takes more than installing infrastructure. It takes an operating model that connects the technology to adoption and business outcomes: bringing users and workloads on board, governing how AI is used, reviewing utilization, and continually identifying the next high-value use case. The goal is to create value early, then build on it. That means measuring use, identifying underutilized capacity, and bringing additional high-value workloads onto the platform over time. Without that discipline, the business may never realize the economic value that justified the investment. With it, AI capacity becomes a productive asset the business can optimize, expand, and use to create measurable value. Three questions to ask Before committing capital, leaders should ask three questions: Is demand becoming steady, predictable, and large enough to justify dedicated capacity? At what level of usage does ownership make economic sense? Can we keep that capacity productive through adoption, governance, and continued use-case expansion? Make the shift deliberately As AI moves into production, the organizations that create the most value will look beyond token prices and the latest model. They will know when recurring demand calls for a different economic model—and they will have the operating discipline to make that capacity productive. That is when AI stops being an expense and becomes an asset. This content was produced by HPE. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

articles.rawFullText: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . Last Wednesday, Anthropic announced that earlier this year it had launched a molecular biology lab, where Claude agents read and conjecture about hard biology problems and human scientists run experiments on what they report. And this AI-powered lab, the company said, had made its first discovery.  To understand what Anthropic says its system did, imagine you’re flipping through a library of millions of DNA sequences, amassed as scientists sequence more and more of the living world. One step toward a breakthrough might be finding a peculiar sequence that encodes an interesting enzyme, perhaps. Then you’d need to figure out what that enzyme does and, eventually, how to manipulate it to do something useful. What Anthropic says its system of 950 agents found after 21 hours was not a brand-new sequence. The agents instead flagged a repeating pattern surrounding a known enzyme, a particular pattern Anthropic said hadn’t been catalogued before. But if you read through Anthropic’s announcement, which calls this pattern “reminiscent” of what led to the gene-editing technology CRISPR that “has already transformed science and medicine,” it sounds as if this army of agents really found something of note.  These claims have angered some biologists. A viral post from one, subsequently endorsed by the chair and CEO of the drugmaker Eli Lilly, said that “finding a weird cluster of genes and repeats is often the easy part. The hard part, and where the real discoveries come from, is figuring out what the system actually does.” The agents helped with some laboratory grunt work, in other words. But a discovery it is not.  It’s a reminder that even if AI does something impressive—like finding a pattern in a mass of biological data that would be difficult to perceive with human eyes alone—the result itself may not constitute a breakthrough for science. What is novel for AI may be routine, unsurprising, or simply not that consequential to a biologist. Muddying the issue further, Mario Rodríguez Mestre, a biologist at the University of Copenhagen, said over the weekend that his team had already discovered this particular pattern, the New York Times reported. Mestre, who regularly chatted with Claude in his work, wondered whether Anthropic’s team had learned from his conversations. Anthropic denies this, but Mestre says he’s stopping all use of Claude anyway. Part of the problem here is that AI companies aren’t presenting their systems simply as tools scientists can use, like microscopes or supercomputers. They’re insisting that the AI systems are making discoveries themselves. To some, that approach is  incompatible with how science actually works, with new knowledge more typically emerging from collaboration and an ever-growing arsenal of tools.  It’s also making people more skeptical of genuine progress when it happens. Whittling 200,000 candidates down to a few worth exploring is no small feat; it is legitimate scientific work. The fact that a general-purpose chatbot could do that work is notable, even if humans helped steer it and ultimately ran the experiments. But once the standard is whether Claude itself made a discovery, all that becomes evidence for one side or the other in a debate that has only two answers: breakthrough or bust. Once we’re judging AI by whether it has made a discovery, it’s also tempting to shift the goalposts even after it really does seem to notch a win. Earlier this month, OpenAI said its own team agents had cracked a million-dollar problem in mathematics. But a couple of weeks later, nearly every AI skeptic in my feed was sharing an article asking whether it was the math problem that really mattered .  To be clear, the piece did not argue that OpenAI’s solution was wrong. Instead, it argued that the particular result may not be the one mathematicians care most about. Throw in the accusation by a mathematician that the models may have used some of his work without credit, and people are left thinking either OpenAI cheated or the solution wasn’t important anyway. Or both. That’s part of what concerns Lucas Harrington, the biologist who wrote the post critiquing Anthropic’s announcement. He closed with a suggestion: AI companies, he said, should “set the bar high now, so that when an AI actually discovers a fundamentally new biological mechanism, everyone appreciates how big a deal it is.” But as OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei race to one-up each other, raising the bar for scientific breakthroughs by AI might be the last thing on their minds.

articles.rawFullText: Listen to the session or watch below The US has spent billions building a “virtual wall” of surveillance towers along its southern border over the past 25 years, promising they will help detect and apprehend border crossers and save lives. But a groundbreaking investigation by MIT Technology Review has documented over a thousand people who moved through areas watched by these towers without being reached or apprehended, and who ultimately died there. Some were even under the watch of newly installed AI-powered towers designed to spot people automatically. Our findings reveal a humanitarian crisis more visible than previously known, and repeated failures of the virtual wall’s basic security promise. Watch a conversation examining the failures of border surveillance technology and uncovering the stories of the people who die in the borderlands. Speakers : Mat Honan , editor in chief, James O’Donnell , senior AI reporter, and Eileen Guo , senior features and investigations reporter Recorded on September 28, 2026 Related Stories The US spent billions on border surveillance. articles.title: 使用LFM2.5-VL-DSpark加速视觉语言模型
articles.originalTitle: Accelerating vision-language models with LFM2.5-VL-DSpark
articles.summary: 这条新闻与模型相关，值得关注其对产品路线、开发者生态或产业竞争格局的影响。原题：Hugging Face：模型相关动态
articles.fullContent: 如何对CPU和GPU上的VLM训练和架构推理加速进行推测性解码视觉工作负载推测的局限性如何使用LFM2. 5-VL-DSpark入门引文今天，我们发布了我们的视觉语言模型(VLM) LFM2. 5-VL-3B的实验性DSpark草案模型。与我们最近发布的LFM2一样。 5-DSpark起草器模型，它添加了一个投机解码路径，在不改变输出质量的情况下，以最小的内存占用增加为更大的加速。视觉起草者使用与我们的文本LFM2. 5-DSpark起草者相同的架构：它捕获目标模型在一组固定的点击层上的隐藏状态和条件，以起草一组k个候选令牌。 图像补丁和文本令牌被投影到这些图层之前的共享表示中，因此无论输入模态如何，起草者都会对相同维度的隐藏状态向量进行操作。因此，推理算法与文本模型保持不变。我们遵循DSpark方案，混合了视觉语言SFT数据，并根据我们期望模型提供的工作负载进行加权。 基于3层、4层和5层的烧蚀，草案模型是一个简化的仅注意力起草器，具有4层和9块大小。我们在最终混合物上运行了10个纪元，并在每个纪元之后测量了验收，在达到递减回报之前，通过额外的训练代币进行了改进。在推断时，我们建议区块大小为8或9 ，具体取决于硬件。 由此产生的起草器具有约2.8亿个参数，并且部署模型的参数计数仅增加8. 9%。LFM2. 5-VL-3B的DSpark草案模型附带对llama. cpp、MLX-VLM和SGLang的第一天支持。我们同时测量设备上的推理和GPU推理。 两种配置都使用DSpark块大小为8 ，并按照MMSpec基准对六种不同的基于视觉的任务进行评估，包括一般VQA、文本VQA、图像字幕、图表VQA、复杂推理和多回合对话。设备上推理。使用M5 Max上的MLX ，解码速度比任务快2. 30倍至3. 13倍。端到端延迟提高了1. 56倍，达到2. 62倍。在M3 Ultra上使用llama. cpp ，解码提高了1. 57倍至2。 14倍，端到端为1. 30倍至1. 77倍。GPU推理。在H100上，同一起草器提供20. 4倍至2. 66倍的解码速度，端到端改进1. 64倍至2. 27倍。在LLM中，预填充主要受计算约束，其成本随提示长度呈二次增长。VLM增加了这一点，因为图像首先通过视觉编码器，然后语言主干处理数百个可视化令牌以及文本提示。 边缘设备的计算量远低于数据中心GPU ，因此预填充占用了更多的端到端延迟，正如Apple silicon和H100上的首次令牌时间和解码测量所显示的那样。（ M5的每核GPU神经加速器缩小了这一差距）。推测解码仅加速解码，而不是视觉编码或预填充。当这些阶段已经占用了大量的墙壁时间时，即使是大的解码加速也只能提供适度的端到端增益。

articles.fullContent: 为什么可重现的评估报告很重要AISI分享的内容为共同的使命做出贡献关于EvalEval联盟关于英国人工智能安全研究所进一步阅读EvalEval联盟很高兴地宣布，英国人工智能安全研究所（ AISI ）正在使用EvalEval的基础设施公开分享评估结果，支持更可重现和可验证的评估科学。 AISI和EvalEval此前曾合作开展研究，该研究始于与NeurIPS 2025一起举办的联合研讨会，该研究所的反馈有助于塑造Every Eval Ever （ EEE ）模式。合作的下一阶段是将共享基础设施付诸实践。随着人工智能部署的加速，评估正成为有关模型和系统性能的越来越重要的证据来源。 然而，许多格式、平台和渠道都报告了结果，但往往没有足够的信息来复制它们。再次进行评估本身可能过于昂贵。EvalEval的使命是通过共享报告架构Every Eval Ever和开放平台Evaluation Cards来改善这一生态系统，该平台将评估结果和解释评估结果所需的信息整合到一个共同的结构中。 这自然建立在AISI的工作基础上，通过OptStop提高评估效率，通过HiBayES提高统计严谨性，并在成绩单分析和能力提取等领域更加标准化。AISI和EvalEval正在共同努力诊断评估报告中的差距，并建立共享基础设施以弥补这些差距。转录水平的透明度不仅关系到重现性，也关系到分析和诊断。 在合作的新阶段， AISI将酌情通过评估卡公开报告评估方法和结果。该版本包括本文主要实验中五个基准的验证结果、上下文和配置信息：这些结果涵盖六个前沿模型： Claude Opus 4、Claude Opus 4. 5、Claude Opus 4. 6、GPT-5、GPT-5. 2和GPT-5. 4。 该版本还包括两个相关的网络评估结果--Cyber CTF和The Last Ones--它们使用了不同的、部分重叠的模型集。这些数据伴随着AISI的论文《推理计算如何塑造前沿法学硕士评估》（ How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation ） ，该论文研究了基准性能如何依赖于推理时间计算和评估协议。Humanity's Last Exam的性能随评估协议和推理计算而变化。 每个曲线显示在给定令牌计数内尝试解决的任务的累积份额，使用最早观察到的每个任务的成功率。当模型在每次尝试后收到来自预言机的正确性反馈时，随着令牌使用的增加，它们会继续解决其他任务。当结果与设置信息一起公开发布时，研究人员和从业人员可以更仔细地研究个体研究，并比较更广泛生态系统的研究结果。 在其他报告缺乏这些细节的情况下，像AISI这样的发布为在上下文中解释评估提供了经过验证的参考点，例如，通过帮助研究人员了解设置选择如何影响报告的绩效。随着越来越多的评估者采用EEE ，像这样的公开比...
